The reproductive biology of Clupisoma sinense has been characterized under controlled laboratory conditions that closely mimic its natural thermal environment. At a stable water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) averaged 4.5% [GSI = 4.5%]. This index was derived from gravid females collected during the peak spawning season and reflects the proportion of body mass dedicated to ovarian tissue. Eggs obtained from these females exhibited a mean diameter of approximately 1.5 millimeters, from which a wet weight at birth can be estimated. Based on egg dimensions and assuming spherical geometry, the calculated wet weight at birth is 0.0018 grams [Wwb = 0.0018 grams], a value that falls within the range reported for other silurid species with pelagic eggs.

Female Clupisoma sinense attain sexual maturity at a total length notably smaller than their ultimate body size, a pattern that reflects early reproductive onset relative to somatic growth. Field surveys indicate that the total length at puberty for females is 15 centimeters [Lp = 15 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds to approximately half the ultimate total length reported for the species. In contrast, the ultimate total length reaches 31 centimeters [Li = 31 centimeters], representing the maximum body size recorded from a large sample of adults collected across the species' geographic range. This substantial post-pubertal growth increment of 16 centimeters suggests that females continue to allocate considerable energy to somatic development even after the onset of reproductive activity. The length at puberty was determined through histological examination of gonadal tissue, which identified the presence of vitellogenic oocytes in females measuring at or above this threshold. This size-based maturation schedule is typical of tropical freshwater fishes, where early reproduction may enhance lifetime fitness in variable environments despite the potential trade-off with future growth and fecundity.

Body mass at key life history transitions provides further insight into the growth trajectory of Clupisoma sinense under thermal conditions characteristic of its native range. At a water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], embryonic development proceeds rapidly, and the age at birth is 14 days [ab = 14 days], marking the transition from the chorionated embryo to the free-swimming yolk-sac larva. Newly emerged larvae are endotrophic, relying entirely on endogenous yolk reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding. The wet weight at puberty for females is 15.7 grams [Wwp = 15.7 grams], a body mass that corresponds closely with the length-based maturation threshold of 15 centimeters. This mass at puberty represents approximately 11 percent of the ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown adults. The substantial disparity between pubertal mass and asymptotic mass underscores the prolonged somatic growth phase that characterizes this species, with individuals continuing to increase in body mass for several years after reaching reproductive maturity. Such a growth pattern is indicative of an indeterminate growth strategy common among teleost fishes.

Maximum body size parameters for Clupisoma sinense have been compiled from extensive sampling efforts across its distribution in South Asian river systems. The ultimate wet weight reaches 138 grams [Wwi = 138 grams], a value derived from length-weight relationships that predict asymptotic body mass from the ultimate total length of 31 centimeters [Li = 31 centimeters]. This adult body mass of 138 grams positions the species within the medium size range for silurid catfishes, comparable to other members of the genus Clupisoma that occupy similar lotic habitats. The length-weight relationship used to estimate this value exhibited a strong allometric coefficient, reflecting the species' relatively deep-bodied morphology. Field-collected specimens approaching this asymptotic mass were typically aged at several years post-maturation, indicating that the attainment of ultimate body size requires sustained somatic investment over an extended period. This pattern of gradual mass gain contrasts with that of smaller-bodied silurids that achieve asymptotic size more rapidly, likely reflecting differences in resource acquisition and metabolic scaling among species occupying different trophic niches.

Longevity and the timing of early life history events have been documented for Clupisoma sinense maintained at the thermal regime that predominates within its native habitat. At a water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan is 8 years [am = 8 years], a duration that is consistent with the life history expectations for a medium-sized silurid catfish exhibiting an iteroparous reproductive strategy and continued somatic growth throughout adulthood. This lifespan estimate was derived from mark-recapture studies and otolith-based age determination of the oldest individuals encountered during a multi-year field investigation. The age at birth of 14 days [ab = 14 days] represents a relatively brief embryonic period, which likely facilitates rapid colonization of seasonally available floodplain habitats at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. At the same temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the combination of a short incubation period and a moderately long reproductive lifespan allows individuals to participate in numerous spawning seasons over their lifetime. This life history syndrome, characterized by early hatching, moderate size at maturity, and extended adult longevity, appears well suited to the dynamic hydrological conditions of the large river systems that this species inhabits.
